case_name: Re Ontario Public Service Employees Union and Forer et al.
text:
Re Ontario Public Service Employees Union and Forer et al.

46 O.R. (2d) 789

10 D.L.R. (4th) 602

ONTARIO

HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE

DIVISIONAL COURT

SAUNDERS, HOLLINGWORTH

AND SMITH JJ.

13TH JULY 1984.

Trade unions -- Members -- Religious exemption -- Jewish employee objecting to resolution of provincial labour federation urging Canadian Labour Congress to call upon Canadian government to recognize Palestine Liberation Organization as legitimate representative of Palestinian people -- Canadian Labour Congress rejecting resolution -- Tribunal granting employee exemption from union dues on basis of religious objection -- Whether tribunal erred -- Crown Employees Collective Bargaining Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 108, s. 16(2).
An individual sought exemption from payment of union dues pursuant to s. 16(2) of the Crown Employees Collective Bargaining Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 108, on the basis of religious convictions. Specifically, he objected to a resolution passed by the Ontario Federation of Labour, of which his union was a member, urging the Canadian Labour Congress to call upon the Canadian government to endorse the Palestine Liberation Organization as the legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. The C.L.C. subsequently rejected the resolution. In the employee's view, the Jewish people had a God-given right to the land of Israel. An exemption was granted by the Ontario Public Service Labour Relations Tribunal. On an application for judicial review, held, Saunders J. dissenting, the application should be granted and the decision quashed.
The meaning of "religious" in s. 16(2) is not one purely subjective to the person seeking exemption. While the employee may have been religiously inspired, the recognition of the P.L.O. as the legitimate representative of the Palestinian people was not a matter of religion per se. Moreover, the tribunal's decision could not stand because of the remoteness of the O.F.L. resolution: the union took no position, and the C.L.C. rejected the thrust of the resolution. Thus, the substratum of the objection had disappeared by the time the tribunal heard the case.
Per Saunders J. dissenting: The determination of the tribunal was essentially factual, and a court should interfere only if the tribunal made an error of law or reached an unreasonable conclusion of fact. It was not unreasonable for the tribunal to conclude that the employee's objection was founded on a religious belief. Moreover, it was not clear that the offensive part of the resolution was dead when the tribunal dealt with the application for exemption. Therefore, the tribunal did not act unreasonably in finding a connection between the employee's religious convictions and his objection to paying dues. The decision of the tribunal did not hamper the union's ability to exercise its rights to freedom of expression and association under the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.
APPLICATION for judicial review of a decision of the Ontario Public Service Labour Relations Tribunal.

Cases referred to
Donald et al. v. Board of Education for City of Hamilton et al.,
1945 CanLII 117 (ON CA)
, [1945] O.R. 518, [1945] 3 D.L.R. 424; Butler v. York University Faculty Ass'n et al., [1981] O.L.R.B. Rep. 1319; Schochet v. OPSEU et al., [1983] O.L.R.B. Rep. 1472
Statutes referred to
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms Crown Employees Collective Bargaining Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 108,   s. 16 Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 228, s. 47(1)

Paul J. J. Cavalluzzo, for applicant.
Chaim Forer, respondent, in person.
D. J. M. Brown, Q.C., for respondent, Ontario Public Service
Labour Relations Tribunal.

SAUNDERS J. (dissenting):-- I have had the benefit of reading
the reasons of Mr. Justice Smith and, regrettably, I am unable
to agree with his conclusion. In setting out my reasons for
reaching a different result, I am afraid there must inevitably
be some repetition.

This application for judicial review of the decision of the
Ontario Public Service Labour Relations Tribunal (the
"Tribunal") to grant to the respondent, Chaim Forer, a
religious exemption is made by the Ontario Public Service
Employees Union ("OPSEU"). The exemption was granted pursuant
to s. 16(2) of the Crown Employees Collective Bargaining Act,
R.S.O. 1980, c. 108. Section 16 provides:

16(1) The parties to a collective agreement may provide for
the payment by the employee of dues or contributions to the
employee organization.

(2) Where the Tribunal is satisfied that an employee
because of his religious convictions or beliefs objects to
paying dues or contributions to an employee organization, the
Tribunal shall order that the provisions of the collective
agreement pertaining thereto do not apply to such employee
and that the employee is not required to pay dues or
contributions to the employee organization, provided that
amounts equivalent thereto are remitted by the employer to a
charitable organization mutually agreed upon by the employee
and the employee organization and failing such agreement then
to such charitable organization registered as such under Part
I of the Income Tax Act (Canada) as may be designated by the
Tribunal.

(3) No collective agreement shall contain a provision which
would require, as a condition of employment, membership in
the employee organization.

Chaim Forer is a public servant covered by a collective
agreement with OPSEU. OPSEU is a member of the Ontario
Federation of Labour (the "OFL") and also of the Canadian
Labour Congress (the "CLC''). At its convention in November,
1982, the OFL passed a resolution dealing with continuing
problems in the Middle East. The resolution urged the CLC to
call upon the Canadian government to support all avenues
towards lasting peace in the region including:

withdrawal of all foreign troops from Lebanon and their
replacement by a United Nations peace-keeping force,

recognition of Israel's right to live within secure borders
based on pre-1967 boundaries,

recognition of the right of the Palestinian people to a
secure and independent homeland,

recognition of the PLO as the legitimate representation of
the Palestinian people.

It is said that the reason the resolution was addressed to
the CLC is because it is the body in the labour movement which
has the authority to pronounce on foreign policy matters. In
January, 1983, the CLC rejected the resolution and reiterated a
position it had previously taken on the Middle East. The
constitution of OFL requires it to support the policies of the
CLC. It is the position of OPSEU that the OFL resolution died
when it was rejected by the CLC.

In the meantime, Forer, in December, 1982, had applied to the
Tribunal for an exemption under s. 16(2) on the following
grounds:

(5) The recent resolution of the OFL (to which OPSEU belongs)
supporting the terrorist PLO in its international war against
the Jewish people is inimical to every human being, in
general, and to every Jew in particular, who believes in the
eternality of the Jewish people and in their God given right
to the land of Israel. It is most obnoxious that I, a
believer, should be required to pay dues to an organization
(OPSEU) whose membership in OFL contributes to OFL's
influence on public opinion in a manner contrary to my belief
and ideas.

The Tribunal in March, 1983, exempted Forer from the payment
of dues for the following brief reasons:

Having regard to the evidence and to the submissions of the
parties and for reasons given in Van Harten v. Civil Services
Ass'n of Ontario (Inc.) et al., July 5, 1976, unreported, it
is our view that the order should be granted. The evidence in
this case is readily distinguishable from the evidence in
Boulakia, 1983, unreported (Ontario Labour Relations Board)
and falls well within the principles enunicated by this
tribunal in previous decisions when exemptions were granted.

In Van Harten v. Civil Services Ass'n of Ontario (Inc.) et
al., decided in 1976, the Tribunal concluded that there must be
a sincerely held religious conviction or belief and a
connection between such conviction and belief and the objection
to paying dues. It stated that the conviction or belief "must,
in the main, be considered from a subjective point of view" and
it was not prepared to question the logic as to how a
particular conviction or belief was arrived at. The Tribunal
did not deal with religious beliefs as contrasted with
political or social beliefs other than to say that it did not
have authority to grant exemptions to religious persons who
"have social or political views unconnected to their
religion which are contrary to those of the employee
organization".

The determination by the Tribunal in a given case is
essentially factual. This court should only interfere if error
is shown of either law or jurisdiction. I would not limit our
power to the case where the Tribunal has made an absurd
finding. However, in my opinion, before exercising our power of
review, we must at least find that the Tribunal made an error
of law or reached an unreasonable conclusion of fact.

The applicant submits that the Tribunal erred in three ways
which may be generally stated as follows:

1. in finding that the objection was religious;

2. in finding a connection between the conviction and beliefs
of Forer and his objection to paying dues as the resolution of
the OFL was at that time, dead; and

3. in not taking into account the competing rights of religion,
expression and association enshrined in the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
.

The characterization of a belief or conviction as religious
must be subjective to a considerable degree. We do not have a
transcript of the evidence before the Tribunal. We do have the
grounds for objection as amplified and explained by the
respondent Forer in the application before us. Shortly stated,
it is his belief, which he founds on scripture, that the Hebrew
people have the exclusive right to occupy and defend Israel
against all comers. I do not recall that he submitted to us
that "everything is religious" as apparently the applicant in
the Humber College case did [Schochet v. OPSEU et al., [1983]
O.L.R.B. Rep. 1472]. There are, no doubt, many who would
characterize his objection to the OFL resolution as the
political views of a religious man. Mr. Forer did, however,
make it clear that his view on the entire situation in the
Middle East was based on a source which he considered to be
divine. It is not for the Tribunal or this court to decide on
some a priori basis what beliefs are capable of being religious
in character.

In Donald et al. v. Board of Education for City of Hamilton
et al.,
1945 CanLII 117 (ON CA)
, [1945] O.R. 518, [1945] 3 D.L.R. 424, the Ontario Court
of Appeal was considering the case of pupils who were
affiliated with the Jehovah's Witnesses and who had refused, on
religious grounds, to participate in school ceremonies
involving saluting of the flag and singing of the national
anthem. They were expelled from school. The question before the
Court was whether these activities were "religious exercises"
within an exemption provided by statute and regulation. One of
the arguments was that the exercises could not reasonably be
said to connote any religious significance. Gillanders J.A.,
with whom Henderson and Roach JJ.A. agreed, stated at pp. 528-9
O.R., pp. 428-9 D.L.R.:

If I were permitted to be guided by my personal views, I
would find it difficult to understand how any well-disposed
person could offer objection to joining in such a salute on
religious or other grounds.

. . . . .

But ... it would be misleading to proceed on any personal
views on what such exercises might include or exclude.

In Butler v. York University Faculty Ass'n et al., [1981]
O.L.R.B. Rep. 1319 at p. 1328, para. 17, it was said for
beliefs or convictions to be characterized as "religious",
that:

... the beliefs must relate to the Divine (in some form) and
man's perceived relationship to the Divine, rather than to
concepts which deal only with man-made institutions and the
relationship of man inter se.

It is noted that in his application for an exemption, Mr.
Forer stated that the recent resolution of the OFL "is inimical
to every Jew who believes in the God given right to the land of
Israel".

The fact that Mr. Forer sincerely and honestly believes the
view which he asserts is not in question. There is no
suggestion that he is attempting to disguise a political
objection as a religious one. While not every sincerely held
religious belief will necessarily result in an exemption, in my
opinion, it was not unreasonable for the Tribunal to have
concluded that the objection of Mr. Forer to the resolution was
founded on a religious belief. There was evidence to support
such a conclusion and we should not interfere with it. I reject
the submission of the applicant that by its finding, the
Tribunal amended the statute by deleting the word "religious"
from s. 16(2).

It is not disputed that there must be some connection between
the conviction and belief and the objection to paying dues. If
there is no evidence of such a connection or if the Tribunal
makes a patently unreasonable finding of a connection, this
court would be entitled to interfere. In my opinion, if a union
passes a resolution that offends the religious belief or
conviction of an employee, it would not be unreasonable for the
Tribunal to find that an exemption should be granted. Here
OPSEU submits not only that it never passed such a resolution,
but that the resolution passed by the OFL is dead. The evidence
is not crystal clear. There is in the applicant's record, but
not in the Tribunal's record, a letter dated January 6, 1983,
addressed to the registrar of the Tribunal from the legal
director of OPSEU, which says in part:

The Union shall also argue that Mr. Forer's application
should be dismissed on the grounds that the resolution to
which he objects was passed by the OFL and not by the Ontario
Public Service Employees Union, and therefore should not be
assumed to represent the policy of the Union in whose
bargaining unit Mr. Forer is a member.

We shall further contend that the policy of the labour
movement as a whole with respect to the PLO is ambiguous,
inasmuch as OPSEU is a member of both the OFL and the CLC
which passed a resolution contrary to that of the OFL once
the decision of the former body became known.

There is also in the applicant's record, but not in the
Tribunal's record, a letter dated January 5, 1983, to the
secretary-treasurer of the OFL from the president of the CLC.
The president of the CLC, in that letter goes no further than
saying that the resolution was the subject of lengthy debate by
the CLC executive council, following which a decison was taken
to reiterate the CLC position on the Middle East. There is an
affidavit of Louis Lenkinski, deposing that the CLC rejected
the OFL resolution and reiterated its position on the Middle
East. There is no evidence that this information was before the
Tribunal. It is to be noted that none of the material before
us, whether before the Tribunal or not, comes out and says that
the OFL motion was put to a vote and was defeated by the CLC.
So far as we are aware, all the Tribunal knew was that the
policy of the labour movement was ambiguous.

Having regard to the material and assuming the information
contained therein was all before the Tribunal, it is not clear
that the offensive part of the resolution was dead when the
Tribunal dealt with the application for exemption. I do not
consider it unreasonable for the Tribunal to have found a
connection between the beliefs and convictions of Forer and his
objection to paying dues.

There is undoubtedly some limit. It is not every objection
that should be found to be connected. This objection may be
borderline but I am unable to say that the Tribunal made an
unreasonable decision.

The final submission of the applicant is to the effect that
the decision of the Tribunal hampers its ability to exercise
its right under the
Charter
to free expression and association.
I do not consider that we should intervene in the decision of
the Tribunal for that reason. There is no restriction on the
applicant union in expressing its views on any subject. If by
doing so it offends the religious beliefs and convictions of
certain employees whom it represents under a collective
agreement, it runs the risk that such employees may object and
be exempted from paying dues. The legislative scheme set out in
s. 16 gives full recognition and scope to the freedoms of
religion, expression and association set out in the Charter.

I would have dismissed the application with costs.

HOLLINGWORTH J. concurs with SMITH J.

SMITH J.:-- This application for judicial review is not free
from difficulty. The Ontario Public Service Employees Union
("Union"), applicant, seeks an order to quash and set aside
a decision by the Ontario Public Service Labour Relations
Tribunal (the "Tribunal") granting a religious exemption to the
respondent, Chaim Forer, from payment of union dues.

The Tribunal's jurisdiction is based upon the provisions of
s-s. 16(2) of the Crown Employees Collective Bargaining Act,
R.S.O. 1980, c. 108 (the Act). They read as follows:

16(2) Where the Tribunal is satisfied that an employee
because of his religious convictions or belief objects to
paying dues or contributions to an employee organization, the
Tribunal shall order that the provisions of the collective
agreement pertaining thereto do not apply to such employee
and that the employee is not required to pay dues or
contributions to the employee organization, provided that
amounts equivalent thereto are remitted by the employer to a
charitable organization mutually agreed upon by the employee
and the employee organization and failing such agreement then
to such charitable organization registered as such under Part
I of the Income Tax Act (Canada) as may be designated by the
Tribunal.

The subsection is nearly identical to s-s. 47(1) of the
Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 228, in so far as its
relevant portion is concerned.

The request for exemption was triggered by a resolution
concerning the Middle East passed at the Convention of the
Ontario Federation of Labour in November, 1982. Leaving aside
the recitals, the resolution was in the following terms:

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the OFL urge the CLC to call
upon the Canadian Government to support all avenues toward
lasting peace in the region including:

withdrawal of all foreign troops from Lebanon and their
replacement by a United Nations peace-keeping force,

recognition of Israel's right to live within secure borders
based on pre-1967 boundaries,

recognition of the right of the Palestinian people to a
secure and independent homeland,

recognition of the PLO as the legitimate representative of
the Palestinian people.

The resolution was forwarded to the Canadian Labour Congress
on December 21, 1982, in the form of a recommendation only. The
congress is the only body under the labour movement's
constitution with authority to pronounce on foreign policy
matters. Upon receipt of the resolution, the congress fully
debated the matter, refused to adopt the resolution and
restated its position paper of August, 1982. The position paper
is decidedly pro-Israel and strongly denounces the PLO as a
terrorist organization and a purveyor of destruction and
hatred.

The request for exemption is in the following terms:

The recent resolution of the OFL (to which OPSEU belongs)
supporting the terrorist PLO in its international war against
the Jewish people is inimical to every human being, in
general, and to every Jew in particular, who believes in the
eternality of the Jewish people and in their God given right
to the land of Israel. It is most obnoxious that I, a
believer, should be required to pay dues to an organization
(OPSEU) whose membership in OFL contributes to OFL's
influence on public opinion in a manner contrary to my belief
and ideals.

The following extract from the Tribunal's decision is a fair
summary of its reasons for allowing the exemption:

Having regard to the evidence and to the submissions of the
parties and for reasons given in Van Harten v. Civil Services
Ass'n of Ontario (Inc.) et al., July 5, 1976, unreported, it
is our view that the order should be granted. The evidence in
this case is readily distinguishable from the evidence in
Boulakia, 1983, unreported (Ontario Labour Relations Board)
and falls well within the principles enunciated by this
tribunal in previous decisions when exemptions were granted.

The mental processes of the Tribunal's chairman as they
relate to his fact-finding function in reaching the conclusion
to which he came, are not made explicit. We are left largely
guessing as to how he defined "religious conviction" in this
particular case and how he became satisfied that "religious
convictions" properly defined, caused the objection.

The problem, of course, is in the use of the adjective
"religious" in the enactment. The word almost defies
definition. It certainly defies exhaustive definition. The
Tribunal's summary treatment of the issue is understandable but
makes the exercise of review a somewhat frustrating one. The
applicant's position is that the Tribunal has interpreted the
word "religious" out of existence and has thereby lost
jurisdiction or at least has ascribed to the word a meaning
which it cannot reasonably bear.

In a very forceful and compelling argument, Mr. Brown has
urged us not to interfere in what is essentially a factual
exercise in which only the Tribunal has the jurisdiction to
engage. With respect, I would find it easier to subscribe to
counsel's position if he were not taking away from the word
"religious" all objective sense. He seemed to betray some
uneasiness in responding, with great ability I might add, to
the various hypotheticals thrown his way. But in the final
analysis, he would only concede to the right or indeed the duty
of this court to intervene in the decision being reviewed if
made on the basis of virtual absurdity. With respect, the cases
cannot be seen to invite deference of that extreme degree.

It seems to me that the legislator could not have intended
the word "religious" to have only the meaning fastened upon it
by the exemption seeker. If it were so, the inquiry would be
limited to a question of degree of sincerity of the person
claiming exemption, regardless of how the conviction was
characterized by any ordinary decent and reasonable member of
the community. There must be a threshold.

Given the particular facts obtaining here, the Tribunal may
well have begged the question when delivering itself of the
short reasons quoted above with nothing more than a simple
reference to the principles enunciated by the same chairman in
Van Harten v. Civil Services Ass'n of Ontario (Inc.) et al.
(July 5, 1976, unreported decision of the Ontario Public
Service Labour Relations Tribunal). Most of what was so ably
said in Van Harten, supra, is helpful in attempting to apply a
concept as ethereal as "religious conviction" to any and
perhaps most given factual situations. That case being entirely
different from the case at hand, the chairman's entreaty to
future tribunals, as embodied in the reasons, to be cautious
not to put an applicant to the condition of satisfying "our
individual views as to what each of us may consider to be
religious", does nothing to advance the resolution of the
problem facing us.

Again we accept readily that religion is subjective and
personal to the person. We also have no doubt as to Mr. Forer's
sincerity.

The troubling feature of this case, however, lies in Mr.
Forer's expressed position that everything is religious. I
pause to say that it is common ground that Mr. Forer was the
only person to give evidence below and we had the benefit of
his statement and submissions when he appeared before us in
person. All other material before the Tribunal was filed with
us at the hearing of this application.

The activities in the Middle East obviously have a religious
dimension. But to deny the political, social and military
realities when interpreting a word like "religious" is to
interpret a statute as would the judiciary in a theocratic
state. We are not concerned with the right or the wrong of Mr.
Forer's views but with whether the security of geographic
boundaries and the military activity with respect thereto are
matters religious and whether a religious conviction in those
regards are what s-s. 16(2) of the Act contemplated.

Mr. Forer may be religiously inspired but in my respectful
view the recognition of the PLO as a legitimate representative
of the Palestinian people is not a matter of religion per se.
We must surely start with a "religious" catalyst (if only in a
most general and minimum objective sense) before going on to
the mind of the objector. Otherwise, the most non-religious or
a-religious pronouncement or act of a trade union could provide
grounds for objection. We cannot accept that the legislator so
intended.

We prefer the approach of the Ontario Labour Relations Board
in Schochet v. OPSEU et al., [1983] O.L.R.B. Rep. 1472, which
is on all fours with the one at bar. The board refused to
accept, as the objector asserted, that "everything is
religious". We recognize that two different administrative
bodies can come to different and opposite conclusions on
essentially the same facts, both of which being beyond judicial
reach. Curial deference can take us that far. Not so here, when
the resolution of the issue turns on the manner of defining the
word "religious".

Another equally cogent reason why the Tribunal's decision
cannot stand lies in the remoteness of the OFL resolution.
OPSEU as such took no position and it is of course the
bargaining agent. Canadian Labour Congress rejected the thrust
of the resolution. The substratum of the "religious objection"
had disappeared by the time the Tribunal heard the matter.

The following comments by the Ontario Labour Relations Board
in the Humber College case [Schochet v. OPSEU] are apposite on
both branches of the union's argument. In other words, they
address both the question of remoteness and the requirement
that the words or actions leading to an objection must have
some measure (viewed objectively) of religious content. I
reproduce them in part for those reasons [at p. 1483, para.
13]:

The applicant is clearly a religious person but a religious
person is capable of giving a patently unreasonable religious
interpretation to an event and thereby assert a personal
feeling or political viewpoint. This, we find, has happened
in the instant matter. While the resolution is objectionable
to the grievor, we must determine whether the claim he
asserts against the respondent is religious in nature. ... of
significance is the fact that his objection could be
withdrawn if OPSEU issued an opposing press release, a fact
suggesting a distinctly political motive. Just as important
is the applicant's unwillingness to acknowledge that OPSEU
itself has no corporate policy dealing with the contents of
the resolution and this board is even unaware of how OPSEU
delegates voted on the resolution. In this context, the
assertion of an objection against OPSEU carries with it the
perception of a non-religious motive -- the achievement of
opposing press coverage through the actions of the only
labour body connected with the OFL over which the applicant
has some bargaining leverage. The refusal of the applicant to
acknowledge and accept that OPSEU is a member of the CLC
which rejected the resolution only adds to this perception.

In the result, the Tribunal erred in principle when
construing s-s. 16(2) of the Act. It cannot possibly or
reasonably be held to apply to the respondent here if it is to
have any meaning at all.

The application is allowed. The decision is quashed. In the
circumstances, there will be no order as to costs.

Application granted.
